Mr. Speaker, a few days
ago the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) asked a question concerning the possible export of potatoes to South Africa. At the time I indicated that I had not the information at hand, but that I would endeavour to obtain it for him. Upon investigation I find that Canadian potatoes have

New Government Loan
been delivered in South Africa to points as far north as Johannesburg. These were seed potatoes. Investigation discloses, further, that potatoes may be transported to South Africa as ordinary cargo, in the ordinary way, although there is no guarantee by shipping companies that they will stand up in transport. Furthermore, the difficulty is that dealers in South Africa are not at all interested in importing potatoes, because they have sufficient for their own requirements. Steamship companies operating to South Africa and those who have looked into the matter carefully are doubtful if potatoes would stand up under ordinary storage conditions. The ocean rate to Cape Town is $11.50 per long ton, in ordinary storage, and $2.50 per hundred pounds if carried in cold storage.
A further report from department officials in South Africa outlines market conditions for eight months of the year. During that time the provinces of Transvaal and the Orange Free State are in a position to supply the whole domestic demand. For the remaining four months the country adjacent to Cape Town supplies the demand, and takes care of the market. For those reasons there is no desire on the part of South African traders to import supplies in competition with the home grown product. That, I think is the gist of the information now before me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: NEW GOVERNMENT LOAN
subsubtopic: REDUCTION OF DENOMINATIONS TO BRING SUBSCRIPTION WITHIN MEANS OF SMALL INVESTOR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the matter to which attention has been brought by my hon. friend was very carefully considered, and the situation very carefully canvassed. In the light of information and advice which came to us from banks and bond dealers as to their experience in connection with similar loans, I felt that inasmuch as this was a very low priced loan and comparatively small, it would be unwise to have smaller denominations in this issue. May I point out to the hon. member that in the national service loan the subscriptions of $100 amounted to less than four per cent of the total amount issued. Obviously it would not be practicable to have the smaller denominations issued in connection with the short-term loan. That would leave a comparatively small loan of $55,000,000 in which to participate. If there were the odd individual who wished to buy a $100 bond, he could do so, for the moment, in the open market. Of course my hon. friend will realize that next year and the year following we shall have very heavy and very large refunding operations before us in hand, and at that time it would be more appropriate to consider the question of bonds of smaller denomination. I might point out to my hon. friend that one consideration was that in connection with the national service loan- I am speaking from memory, but I think accurately-although the total subscriptions for the smaller amounts were less than four per cent of the total issue, the cost of handling the coupons, the labour employed in servicing the bonds is greater for that four per cent than it is for the remaining 96 per cent. That was also borne in mind. So for the reasons that I have indicated it was thought unwise at this time to issue the smaller denominations.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, November 8, consideration of the motion of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett (Prime Minister) for the second reading of Bill No. 8, an act respecting a certain trade agreement between His Majesty's government in Canada and his Majesty's government in the United Kingdom.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister made his highly militant and denunciatory speech last Thursday, he could not have expected that he was contributing much towards shortening this debate. In that speech he

invited many hon. members to go back to their constituents and tell them that they had opposed this and that and the other thing. I do not want to take that too much as a challenge, but it was an invitation at all events, made in such a tone as to indicate that he thought we were afraid to do so. But these matters were all taken into consideration before the debate was started, as soon as we came to this house and saw what was before us. So we will have no hesitation, not only in accepting that invitation, but in this house endeavouring once more to give the reasons why we are opposed to this agreement now under discussion. AVe have been giving reasons for three weeks, some of them categorically, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) gave fourteen different reasons, in a good speech associated therewith; the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Butcher) confined his statement to something like six specific reasons, and every member on this side of the house who spoke, those representing the Liberal party at all events, gave specific and substantial reasons why he could not see his way to support this agreement.
If I were confined to one or two minutes in giving my reasons I would quote from Mr. Baldwin's opening address, the words which have been quoted several times already in this debate, to the effect that there are two ways of promoting preference and interimperial trade; one by reducing tariffs between the various units of the British commonwealth of nations, the other by raising tariffs against the rest of the world. And Mr. Baldwin indicated that he would very much prefer the former way. That is exactly where we on this side of the house stand. That alone would be a sufficient reason for me By lowering tariffs you not only promote trade, you increase revenue and also make goods cheaper to the consumers of this country, and no doubt they need it. By raising tariffs against the world-and we have had a double raising of tariffs by 'hon. gentlemen opposite, not only against the world but also against Great Britain-you throttle trade, decrease revenue and make goods dearer to the people of Canada. But as I am not confined to one or two minutes I am glad of the opportunity to take up some further phases of the question.
It is a very dangerous thing to attribute motives to anyone. How are we to know the motives of other hon. gentlemen? AVe may know our own motives, but it is not safe, especially for a lawyer, to impute motives to anyone else. He is always caught up very

United Kingdom
quickly by the lawyer on the other side, and sometimes by the judge, when he indulges in such a questionable practice. I remember as a boy I often used to hear the old answer, when one imputed base motives to another: You are measuring your corn in the other's half bushel. So I am afraid the Prime Minister was measuring his corn in that other one's half bushel; in other words, judging the other party by himself. Yet I believe he did an injustice to himself by putting himself in that position. I scarcely think so ill of the Prime Minister as that. I suppose in the right hon. gentleman's practice before the courts, when he found he had a weak case the plan was to abuse the other fellow's attorney. But that was played out long ago, and I am surprised that anyone occupying his high position and with his remarkable powers of oratory and of expression should resort to that worn out and questionable method.
Another reason why we so much resent that particular speech is that the right hon. gentleman cast imputations upon our old and esteemed leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, that were absolutely without foundation. That point was so well dealt with by my .right hon. leader last night that I only refer to it in passing.
I am familiar with the story of the British preference, not in this parliament it is true, but by following it carefully ever since the preference was initiated in 1897. The statement made by the right hon. Prime Minister, it seems to me, was entirely apart from the facts. I could scarcely believe my ears when I heard his recital of what he represented to be the facts of the matter. You would wonder that anyone in a condition of sanity would make such a statement.
Let me turn to the two conferences that are under discussion. One links in with the other, because one is claimed to be based on the other. With respect to the conference of 1930, let us refresh our memory. I will not read much because I think the house is very familiar with the story, but just the crucial statement:
I (Mr. Bennett) offer to the mother country, and to all the other parts of empire, a preference in the Canadian market in exchange for a like preference in theirs, based upon the addition of a ten per centum increase in prevailing general tariffs, or upon tariffs yet to be created. In the universal acceptance of this offer, and in like proposals and acceptances by all the other parts of the empire, we attain to the ideal of empire preference.
Then he elaborates thus:
In the first place, the rate I have mentioned cannot be uniformly applied. The basis of the proposal is the adequate protection to industries now existent, or yet to he established.
Adequate protection, that is the basis of this offer. A few paragraphs prior to that he said:
Projects other than the one I propose have been placed before you. They have been carefully canvassed by our delegation, and, while we would avoid anything which might savour of premature condemnation, we are constrained to state that none of them can be accepted by Canada as alternatives at all likely to achieve the purpose we have in mind.
So eight days after the conference convened in London we have our Prime Minister practically issuing an ultimatum to the conference that any alternative proposals cannot be considered; his and his only must be accepted, or there is nothing doing, unless it is based upon protection.
Now turning to my right hon. friend's speech of the twelfth of October, at the submission of the resolution, after enumerating the various agreements that have been come to, there is this statement:
These agreements mark the first forward step in a definite scheme of closer empire economic association.
The first forward step. That would cause amazement, I am sure, even among the Prime Minister's followers. I wonder how many think that helps his case. A stranger in the gallery listening to that would think this was the first step towards British preferenice made by any living man or by any government. There is nothing associated with that statement to indicate otherwise. I have read it all over, and if the Prime Minister had said that this was the last backward step in the promotion of inter-empire trade, by raising tariffs against the British people and still higher tariffs against the world, I could have agreed with him. My right hon. leader went so fully into that question last night that I merely refer to it to indicate the folly and falsity of that statement. It carries its own refutation. Let us proceed:
They (the Ottawa proposals) are based upon the principle enunciated by the Conservative party before the last general election, and steadfastly supported by it from that time to the present. They conform to the general plan proposed by this government at the economic conference held at London two years ago. . . .
That is the London conference to which I have just referred. The foundation of this agreement is adequate protection, and for that reason I am opposed to it.
Let me refer briefly to another great objection that has arisen. You know, Mr. Speaker, as a party we never have been in favour of these hard and fast, cat and dog bargaining agreements. That is what we have here, if we are to believe half the evidence we hear.

Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
Another regrettable incident in connection with these discussions was the remark made by Neville Chamberlain with respect to the ties of empire wearing thin in Canada. I do not want to say anything derogatory of that gentleman, but if ever there was a foolish and mischievous remark it was the one he made. I think I am warranted in making that statement, and it was simply the result of this kind of bargaining and of endeavouring to defend its conclusions. Over in England they must make some attempt to justify themselves, and they forget that what they say there is reported here the following morning. Their remarks sound differently here. I am not going to quote what Mr. Chamberlain said; I would not be so cruel, but he intimated that the ties of empire were wearing so thin that they required something to bolster them up. Our ties may be wearing thin; all the rest of our clothes may be wearing thin, but that does not apply to the ties to which he referred. His father did not say that. His father was the author of that famous statement to the effect that the silken ties of kinship are stronger than ties of iron. That still holds true with a large body of the people of Canada who own Great Britain as their motherland.
That same gentleman, Mr. Chamberlain, made another very foolish statement. Apparently he was fearful lest the United States would tie up to us if Great Britain did not tie up first. That is a very provocative and mischievous statement, but I am not astonished at it. I do not feel like blaming him; when our own Prime Minister has indulged in that kind of clap-trap what can we expect from Neville Chamberlain?

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
That is what I think he did, and he must have been pretty well primed. This newspaper I have-the Belfast Post-is almost worn out. I am not going to harass the feelings of the Tories over there by reading very much from it, but here we have their leader all gowned and decked with honours-and well deserved honours, too- when he received an honorary degree from Belfast university. The right hon. gentleman made a speech on that occasion, and I do not see that it possibly could be termed anything other than an attempt at straight intimidation of our overseas kinsman. He said that if empire ties were not strengthened economically the old empire would blow up. The heading is "Empire Ties must be Economic." The article goes on:
(Mr. Motherwell.]
"I am satisfied," he said, speaking at the luncheon, "that if we do not avail ourselves of the matchless opportunity that we have by reason of our far-flung empire, our fate will be the fate of other great empires of the past."
We know what happened to the older empires referred to; they went to pieces, and the Prime Minister said we must tie ourselves up by means of tariffs because the other ties are gone. He continued:
While sentiment, he asserted, must always blaze a pathway, the ties that bound peoples to one another at the present day must be ties of material strands of economic strength.
But in my opinion when we have to rely upon high tariff ties of this description to tie us to the motherland the end is not far away.
Lest I may have given a wrong interpretation to these words of our Prime Minister or put a construction upon them that never was meant by the right hon. gentleman, let me refer to an editorial which appeared in the same Belfast tory paper about a week later. Apparently it took them about a week to recover from the shock. Those were astonishing statements he made, and he even brought in the famous Boston tea party as a means of further intimidation, holding it up as a spectre, as though he were saying that if something were not scon done there would be another Boston tea party. I quote from the editorial:
After the cold and didactic speeches in Belfast a few days ago of Mr. Bennett, the Canadian premier, who asserted that the old ties of blood and kinship between motherland and dominions were broken, and that if not replaced by commercial ties, "the empire would share the fate of the great empires of the past," it was heartening to hear Mr. Scullin speak of those old ties as still existent and still strong. "The unity of the commonwealth of nations," he declared, "lies in the blood ties that exist between the various parts." We would much rather take that hopeful view than the gloomy one of Mr. Bennett.
Mr. Scullin, the Australian Prime Minister, had also spoken in Belfast about the same time, and they bad an opportunity to compare the two gentlemen. Now we can understand why Mr. Chamberlain makes these nonsensical, rattle-brained statements with regard to the empire ties wearing thin. Now it is easy to understand why we resent that kind of talk, and that is what this sort -of "dog-fight" bargaining has led to. What will it be like when we have two or three more conferences? I will wager that not one of the gentlemen from abroad who attended the last Ottawa conference will attend another conference in Canada so long as the present government is in power. They will take no more chances.

They could not come barehanded here after their experience with our diplomatic quartette to London in 1930; hence the British delegates equipped themselves the way they did for the 1932 event. The Right Hon. Mr. Thomas referred to this sort of preference as humbug. Some people thought that his use of that word was a diplomatic blunder, but in my opinion it was the naked truth and a very happy expression. But if the first conference was humbug, what sort of language should be used to describe properly the last conference? Surely it must have been the diouble-dyed, twice-distilled quintessence of humbug, sham and pretence so far as the juggling with our Canadian tariff was concerned.
Another objection I have is this. I have been warning against imputing motives, but I can come to no other conclusion than that in this agreement under the guise of preferences, Canadian tariffs have been put up against the world and pegged there for five years; and not only have they been put up against the world but the leaders on the ministerial side, including the Prime Minister, have gone about boasting publicly that the outside world will have to pay tribute to the British Empire for the privilege of trading with us in the future. Can you imagine anything like that? Should hon. gentlemen of that description be left running at large in this critical period? Plowever, we have some hope. Judging from the corralling of some of these high tariff gentlemen to the south of us yesterday, I think we have reason to believe that gentlemen of the same type on this side will not be at large very long.
Now I will refer to the wheat question. In this regard the right hon. gentleman opposite challenged me to go back to Saskatchewan and defend the position I have taken. Well, if ever there was a piece of sham and pretence it is the wheat preference that has been extended to us. I have not heard any of the western Tories defend it yet. We had one or two very good speeches from them. We had a speech from the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, but I must say that I did not hear him defend the "world price" proviso attached to the so-called wheat preference, although I heard him upbraiding myself a Jittle bit; and the hon. member for Souris also made a good speech, but he took pains not to mention the fatal rider to the wheat preference. This is another instance of each of them

-Canada and the United Kingdom-dragooning the other. At the last moment of the conference, when everyone thought that the wheat question was settled, and word had gone abroad throughout the land through the press that there would be no wheat quotas, or preferences, lo and behold, our Prime Minister, against the advice of expert advisers on both sides of the water, insisted upon a wheat preference. From what we can gather, it was going to blow up the whole works if he insisted on that and got a real preference, because the Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin did not wish to expose his political flank to the attacks of the home Labour party and the Liberal party by leaving himself open to the accusation that he was making the poor man's loaf any dearer. Consequently we got a nominal preference with one hand, from the Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin, at the instance of our Prime Minister, and then with the other hand Mr. Baldwin took it away by saying that we must supply wheat at world prices-exactly what we have been doing for over fifty years. I wonder how many people they hope to humbug by that procedure. I will tell you what it has enabled the Tories in Canada to do. When the Prime Minister was speaking last Thursday he never mentioned that fatal rider which says that we will just get what we have been getting. That kind of preference does not amount to a hill of beans. When the Prime Minister was speaking on the resolution on October 12 he admitted that he had never promised the Canadian farmer that he would raise the price of wheat by this preference and consequently raise the price of bread in the old country. He said he believed that this measure would enable the farmers of the west to have a secure market in which to sell larger quantities. Where is the evidence of that? The only way we can sell larger quantities of wheat in Great Britain is by means of the quota. There is no assurance under this present arrangement that we will be able to sell one bushel more.
I wonder what my good friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) was thinking of when he did not have decided decisively the matter of wheat routings through Buffalo or other American ports. Apparently the government never thought about this matter although practically three-fifths of our east-bound wheat goes via Buffalo. According to a cablegram received from the Hon. Mr. Howard Ferguson, wheat reconsigned through the United States to England will not be given the benefit of the British preference. However, this wheat is not losing very much on that account. Such wheat is to be treated,

United Kingdom
however, as foreign and taxed six cents import duty before it can enter Great Britain. I am hopeful that the United Kingdom will decide not to so penalize this trade route which has been used advantageously between Canada and Great Britain for the last fifty years. The leader of the government attempts to shirk all responsibility in connection with this matter by stating that the British government has the administration of this matter.
He did not leave it entirely to the British government to rescind or abrogate the Russian treaty. If he was as careful of the western farmer as he is in giving another knock to Russia, he would have seen that our wheat would have been permitted to go via Buffalo and still be treated as Canadian wheat. This wheat will now be forced into unnatural channels via Halifax or St. John and the cost of transportation will be increased. There will be increased freight rates, canal charges and ocean rates to contend with, to say nothing of the additional storage space which will have to be provided at our Atlantic ports. As everyone knows, the elevators at Buffalo are used primarily for storage purposes. The wheat is crowded forward in the fall of the year while the lakes are still open in order to be as near tidewater as possible during the winter. I do not think there is one hon. member in this house but would favour our Canadian ports being patronized, but I, for one, am not prepared, nor can we afford, to pay four or five cents more per bushel in order to have our wheat routed that way. If we could get a reduction in freight rates to permit of it, it would be different, but we are now faced with these alternative penalties which have been imposed on us by this government in agreement with the British government. Who signed the Anglo-Canadian treaty? It was the right hon. the Prime Minister and Mr. Chamberlain and yet as a signatory to the treaty, the Prime Minister attempts to deny responsibility and places the whole blame upon the British government. He has no defence in this connection.
I should like to refer to what I would term a sin of omission, the lack of consideration of the monetary question. How can we hope to promote interempire trade when we have been piling tariffs one on top of another for the last two years? In addition to these tariffs we are faced with an adverse exchange rate which is equivalent to a duty of twenty-five per cent against all our goods entering Great Britain. It is an utter impossibility to trade under these conditions. One of the first things to do in order to improve the course of a
stream or ditch is to remove all obstructions, such as old dams, brush, logs or other debris. Sometimes it is necessary to deepen the ditch, but at other times the removal of obstructions is sufficient to increase the flow. One of the main obstructions which should have been removed in connection with our trade stream was the adverse exchange. Every animal, every bushel of wheat and every other commodity sent to Great Britain is penalized to the extent of twenty-five per cent adverse exchange, and that is one of the reasons why our cattle and hogs can scarcely find a market over there. If we were on the strict export basis in bacon now we would be getting almost one cent less than we are at the present time for our live hogs. In the face of all this the right hon. gentleman continues to spin yarns by the mile expatiating upon the wonders of this agreement.
If this exchange question could not be corrected at a family gathering of British dominions, how is it going to be corrected at the world conference of strangers to be held at some unknown date and in some unknown place? In the meantime we have to suffer. I wonder if the government has ever heard of that old saying: While the oats are growing, the horse is starving to death. I wonder if the government realizes the distressing condition of agriculture in the west? Instead of engaging in these impossible, abortive ways of improving our markets, ways which cannot help but be disappointing, the government should try to work out some plan to remedy the wheat glut situation. A gentleman by the name of C. AV. Petersen, the editor of the Farm and Ranch Review of Calgary has, in my opinion, suggested a very useful basis of solution of this problem. He recommends a world conference of the great wheat growing and exporting countries. These are the United State, Canada, the Argentine and Australia, but there is still another and that is the fly in the ointment-Russia. I believe that the suggestion put forth by this gentleman is possible of some development. Whether or not we like it, our wheat production must be reduced to near the world's capacity to consume. Otherwise the situation will continue to get worse and worse. Our carryover is becoming larger each year. I recognize the fact that no one country could afford to reduce its wheat acreage without similar action being taken by the others. Should an agreement be reached by these five countries, including Russia, I would look for something in the way of a systematic reduction of the tremendous overages occurring or increasing each year. The overage from last year added to the crop of this year, gives Canada alone

That will be the result of the ruthless law of the survival of the fittest. What stands in the way of a solution of this problem? Russia. What stands in the way of Russia plajdng the game with the rest of the exporting countries? The attitude of this government towards Russia hitting them an embargo swat in the eye every time they get an opportunity. Russia is a nation with the largest white population in the would, trying to work out its own destiny, in a way different from ours, it is true; but if we are democratic, if we believe in self-government, why cannot we let them have the right to govern themselves in their own way? I do not believe in sovietism any more than does anyone else, buit I believe they have a right to work out their own destiny-a right which Canada claimed and exercised. A futile attempt was made to cooperate with Russia a year and a half ago. The Hon. Howard Ferguson was sent to Rome to negotiate with Russia on the wheat question. That was just a short time after we had placed an embargo on a number of her exports. What kind of setting was that to get satisfactory results? It was another hare-brained method of trying to secure something by the blasting or blazing route. Since then every Russian knows it was at the instance of Canada that this treaty between Great Britain and Russia was abrogated recently. What kind of feeling will the Russians now have towards Canada? As a matter of fact, as I see it, by again thus swatting Russia in the eye, our government have spiked the one possible chance in sight of securing joint action by the five great wheat exporting countries of the world looking towards the reduction of wheat acreages to meet present day consumption requirements.

I ask them to show courage and not to. be school children, to tell the Prime Minister about the misery of the people. Hon. gentlemen opposite have a real opportunity; they meet him in caucus, they can speak to him in his office or in the house, and they must tell the Prime Minister that he is ruining the trade of this country. We need a moderate tariff in order that we may exchange goods with other countries, and hon. gentlemen opposite must tell that to the Prime Minister.
The right hon. gentleman has a very strong voice; he uses it in order that people will not know that his knees are trembling. When he is afraid, he uses his voice to impress his supporters. No one should be afraid of him. He has nothing but his voice with which to impress people. He has a strong voice and a nice appearance, but that is all. Hon. members opposite should not bother the Prime Minister too much in regard to questions of patronage. They should not stay so close around him; they should remember the bees, who kill their queen with love. Hon. gentlemen opposite surround the Prime Minister; they are very close to him; they hold him so tightly that he has no chance to rest or to think. They surround him as flies surround molasses. They should give the right hon. gentleman a chance to breathe, a chance to think. He is a very clever lawyer; he honours our profession. He can think, if they will give

him a chance to do so, but they are always around asking him to give the Postmaster General authority to cut the throats cf small postmasters.
I see my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) across the way, with a genial smile. He was far away during the last session. Now that he is here and is friendly with the Prime Minister, let him be helpful to that right hon. gentleman. Let him be one of the Prime Minister's bodyguard, so that he may help to keep at some distance those who do not give the right hon. gentleman a chance to sleep or to rest, and who are responsible for his overworking-eighteen hours a day, I believe. Surely the Prime Minister needs some sleep; he should sleep at least eight hours in the twenty-four. He should have some ti-me for rest and for meals. They must give him a chance; they must be reasonable. He may be a superman but he needs eight hours of sleep just the same. And he must eat, and relax. I say, they should give him a chance to regain his natural happy disposition. Then he will be able to think, and it will be the proper time then for hon. gentlemen opposite to make representations to their leader on behalf of the civil servants and of the poor and the unemployed. They ought to say to him, "Dear R. B., Why do you not extend your sympathy to these poor unemployed? Why do you not try to live up to your promises of 1930, when you said that you would end unemployment and that prosperity would be restored as soon as you got into power?" That would be very nice. God has always prevented me from being a Tory, and I am thankful for that, but if I were on the other side of the house I would speak exactly in those terms to the right hon. gentleman. But no one on the other side has the courage to urge upon the Prime Minister that he give some consideration to the poor, to the humble, to all those who are suffering. They have not the courage to ask him to come to the rescue of those people in order that their lives may be made happier and in order that our present troubles may be overcome. I repeat, it is because not one of them has had the courage to make such representations to the Prime Minister that he has persisted in this stupid policy of high tariffs; and it is because I regard that policy as stupid that I vote against it. I would say this to the Prime Minister's face, if he were here today, honouring us with his presence, but he is away and I must say it in any case. I am glad to have learned from him yesterday that he is reading Hansard. I hope he will continue to read it, but if he does not read it

I am going to take the words of a man who has been quoted as an authority, again and again in this house, the words of a man who was imported by' the Prime Minister to Canada for the purpose of conducting an investigation, a man whom the Prime Minister on public platforms and in private conversations has praised again and again. I shall give the name later because I do not wish the value of his words to be lost. Listen to this:
Canada's economic dependence upon world prices is greater than ever. It was sometimes thought her decision to adhere to some fixed relation for her currency to the New York dollar as distinct from the opposite course of adopting sterling or some intermediate level rested upon the importance to the dominion of avoiding payment of substantial premiums on her heavy New York obligations. It had been said Canada could not possibly afford this premium or its general effect upon her credit. This dilemma is more apparent than real. Even if Canada left her present dollar standard and her internal price level rose, she would still have to pay her New York obligations and with gold prices raised abroad for her wheat, the relation between the Canadian dollar and the New York dollar would become immaterial for the purposes of payment.
Those are the words of Sir Josiah Stamp. Let hon. members hear them now, and think them over.

speechtext: When was that statement made?

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I have read from a Canadian Press cable dated at Lon-

don, May 23, That some action of this kind is imperative must be clear to every hon. member opposite. Why, their own leaders are now talking glibly and fatuously about the necessity for a rise in price level, but they will not take the only means by' which that rise may be brought about. They' refuse to. They say, "Oh no, we cannot do that; we are on a sound money basis." I say to them that as long as they insist upon staying on a so-called sound money basis and tying Canadian internal and external monetary-matters to New York, they cannot raise price levels unless New York does. They are tied definitely to the New York money policy. Our monetary- policy for years has been governed pretty well by that of the United States federal reserve. As an hon. member said in this house not long ago, w-e are regarded on Wall street as the thirteenth federal reserve district, with this difference, that the other twelve districts have a voice in the policy, and Canada has not.
That condition of affairs which has prevailed due in part to the absence of the establishment of a central publicly owned and directed bank in Canada, will prevail as long as this government's avowed policy of so-called sound money continues. Prices must rise-well, if they do not rise there must be a general cancellation, or, worse still, a general repudiation of debts; we cannot meet our obligations. Let us take a look at the picture, Mr. Speaker. In Great Britain, France, Australia, Italy, India-anywhere-the great demand at the moment is for a rising price level. Because of what? Because of a mad monetary and economic system which is placing upon the backs of the common people all over the world the intolerable and unbearable burden of debts. Study the history of any borough in England; study the history of any state of the union; take the financial statement of any province in Canada and read the story. There is but one picture. Let us go back one hundred, twenty-five, ten or even five y-ears ago, and we will find that from year to year there has been a story of steadily growing debt, steadily piling up of fixed obligations reaching an aggregate which staggers the imagination. W'e hear talk of an attempt to meet those obligations today-. With the prevailing price levels of commodities I tell y-ou it is impossible. Why, the world's gold bearing obligations alone are over five hundred billion dollars, and there is only eleven billion of monetary- gold in all the world. The thing is a farce. So it is not surprising that those who have some interest in economics and less in politics, who have studied these problems, are now- expressing

United Kingdom
the views which have been expressed by men who have been trying to find a road which would lead to a betterment of the condition of Canadian people.
I have in my hand the words of Dr. Marvin of the Royal Bank, who says that as prices have continued to fall the burden of debts has been increased by from fifty to seventy-five per cent.
Then I read the following statement:
It is coming to be realized that there must be a major rise in prices or there will be heavy cancellations of a substantial proportion of such obligations.
Then he follows with a closing paragraph which I draw to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes):
One thing or another is inevitable; prices must rise or there will be a wholesale cancellation or repudiation of such debts. For the same reason a continuation of the present price level will bring on wholesale bankruptcy.
The facts are before hon. members opposite, and they may do what they wish about it. But already even their Tory colleagues in Great Britain are beginning to see the light. Imagine my astonishment, and that of those who have been preaching this gospel for some years, when we find coming to the support, not of our detailed policy but of part of it, no less a personage than Lord Beaverbrook. I almost apologize for quoting his words.

speechtext:
After reading the economic monstrosities of which he has been guilty, I cannot imagine that anything that Lord Beaverbrook would say can be of value. Yet these words of his are so apropos at the moment that they have a value. This is not an editorial. I quoted on a former occasion an editorial from the Daily Express of April 13. These are Lord Beaverbrook's own words, from an article which he himself wrote in the Daily Express subsequent to that time:
It should be our policy to make money both plentiful and cheaper. It may be fairly cheap at the moment. I do not deny that. It is certainly not plentiful. Until we have made it plentiful we will not be able to maintain the standard of wages here.
How can it be made plentiful? Send the Bank of England about its business! Let it continue to perform the functions of a joint stock bank.
Establish a central bank, owned by the nation, equipped with all the powers necessary to provide abundant credi-t and hedged about by all the restrictions required to safeguard the permanence and stability of the structure. That is the solution. Give us the right to establish reasonable credit and sufficient banking facilities for the people, and you will get
the present wage 'level, stability of commodity prices and prosperity for our people. Give us that authority and you will get the restoration of the cuts.
If you believe in the policy, join our movement. If you do not want it, do what you can to destroy us!
The same words may be directed to hon. gentlemen opposite-well I do not think they will destroy anything by not joining it; I think rather they will destroy anything by joining it. Frankly I would rather not have them as long as they hold their present point of view on these matters.
But hon. members are frightened by this bogy of inflation, this ghost that they conjure up to wriggle in front of them; they see Germany, they see Russia, they see all sorts of things, forgetting there is no analogy. If they were fair in their examination of the proposals they would say: Yes, inflation does not need to be the mad thing it was in Germany. In France, it was not. France undertook an intelligent form of inflation, under which she cleaned off her internal debts, established the franc at a value far below its pre-war value, and placed herself in such a position that she was able to act as an instrument which nearly destroyed Great Britain's financial power. She is an example of a country which undertook intelligent inflation. We could do the same, we could manage inflation. But remember, even France has not escaped, because the French policy of banking did not extend to the rational internal economic planning that is a necessary part of a managed currency policy. The two have to go hand in hand. I am however discussing merely inflation at the moment, Hon. gentlemen should not forget that the late C. E. Neill, general manager of the Royal Bank of Canada, in the last annual statement he was able to deliver, pointed out that the only way by which the price level could be restored was by inflating the purchasing power and credit and currency of the country. Not only that, but he goes further and says that it is the denial of intelligence to assert that one cannot achieve stability of price level, and in illustration of that he says: overproduction of agricultural products in relation to manufactured articles would justify a decline in the price level, but when the average of all prices declines this can only be explained by an under supply of that in which prices are expressed, i.e. money, and it would seem that ii the effective supply of money is kept in the right relation to production of commodities, the phenomenon of a declining average price level will not occur.
Those are not my words, they are not the words of hon. members around me, they are

It was made clear originally that their staying the in the cabinet did not imply support of duties which were being proposed for preference purposes. In the dispatch referring to the recent order in council it was stated that, as a matter of fact, it was thought that the original purpose already had been largely served; that the act had been passed, amongst other reasons, for the purpose of balancing their trade, and that trade had come to be pretty well balanced through what the measure had already accomplished.

It was also made clear at the time the Import Duties Act was passed that Great Britain certainly would be free to grant to any other country the exemptions which were being granted the dominions under this act. I hold in my hand a copy of an article that appeared in the London Spectator of October 8, 1932. Here is what the Spectator says in regard to the right of Great Britain to give to any other nation the exemption from general duties which she is giving the dominions:
As for the astonishing Canadian contention that we are bound to maintain tariffs against foreign countries, not merely on the specific articles on which Canada is promised a preference but on the whole range of commodities on which we have imposed any duties at all, that is too untenable to call for serious comment.
The Spectator uses the words, "too untenable to call for serious comment" in referring to which it describes as "the astonishing Canadian contention" which has been put forth from some quarters and which, if I am not mistaken, the hon the Minister of Trade and Commerce is attempting to convey at the moment. It is not going to help in accomplishing the ends of this agreement if the House of Commons does not understand at this stage exactly what we are getting. One of our objections to this method of negotiating, is that it is likely to give rise to endless differences of opinion as to what has and what has not been granted. I say it will be better for all concerned if, as we go through these articles one by one, we understand clearly and exactly just what they mean. We do not desire this for the purpose of scoring any political point, but for the purpose of understanding exactly what these agreements mean and imply. More than that, if hon. members have read the analysis given in the Economist and other papers in Great Britain with regard to the agreements, they will see that, over and over again, the English writers who have reviewed the agreement have said emphatically that, with regard to the whole range of commodities, with the exception of a few which are specifically guaranteed under the agreements, Britain is free to give to nation A, nation B, nation C, nation D and so on, exactly the same thing she is giving the dominions in the way of exemption from any or all of the general duties. More than that, the United Kingdom committee which has been preparing for the world economic conference has been discussing this very matter. As some hon. gentlemen may have noticed, Sir Walter Layton resigned from that committee only a day or two ago because he said he had been instructed by the Chancellor of the Exchequer that at the world
economic conference an effort would be made to arrange to give additional preferences to other nations in much the same way as the dominions were being given exemptions. Sir Walter Layton felt this would not permit sufficiently of the removal of tariff barriers, as such an arrangement contemplated still keeping the tariff for protective purposes. May I say just a word or two on the matters to which the right hon. gentleman has spoken? In the first place he has been dealing with the question of the motives which lay behind the Import Duties Act. I

cannot see any relevancy in the matter of the motives. So far as Canada is concerned, the benefits are the same whatever were the motives behind the Import Duties Act when it was passed. The benefits which we receive in Canada under the treaty are free entry for certain goods, and the benefits of that free entry are not at all depreciated or diminished if the motives of Great Britain in passing the Import Duties Aet originally were the one thing or the other. The benefits are precisely the same.
But when the right hon. gentleman produces to this house as the authority for his statement that the motive of the British government in passing the Import Duties Act was purely the raising of revenue and, with an absolute disregard for all constitutional law, of which he is usually a champion, tries to persuade this house-I am perfectly certain he did not persuade himself-that a statement by a private member of the British house was to outweigh and to render of absolutely no effect or meaning the clear statement of the act itself in its preamble, then he is asking the house to do a thing which no ordinary member is prepared to do whether he is a lawyer or not. Then the right hon. gentleman, taxed with the absurdity of this argument, asked the house to listen to what the Right Hon. Mr. Thomas had said, to support the statement and explanation made by the private member. There is not a single statement made which the hon. gentleman read as from the lips of Mr. Thomas that supports the motive that was represented and submitted by the private member. Mr. Thomas does not state that the Import Duties Act was introduced for the purpose of balancing the budget or that it was a matter of raising revenue. Mr. Thomas states that the purpose of the Import Duties Act was strictly in relation to the question of interimperial preferences. The undertaking is to maintain the present preferential margin. Let me explain this schedule very briefly in order that the committee may get the background of it. During the conference, when these very important matter were under discussion, it was disclosed, indeed it had already been known, that the British government had some months before appointed a commission to study the pig industry of Great Britain. The object of that commission was to ascertain what was the beet thing to do to stimulate that industry, and to anyone who knows the adaptability of that country to the raising of pigs, and also the large quantities of pig products imported into Great Britain, it will be apparent at once that it is desirable to develop that industry. This commission was still holding its hearings, and it was expected that possibly some recommendations might be made which would call for a protective measure-we at any rate would use the term in that sense-for the benefit of the British pig industry. To that we have no objection, provided, as indicated here, the preferential margins are maintained; and so, in drafting
this schedule, the language used here was regarded as the most apt to express the views in the light of that contingency. His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom will invite parliament to pass the legislation necessary to impose on the foreign goods specified in schedule B appended hereto, the duties of customs shown in that schedule in place of the duties (if any) now leviable.

speechtext: And schedule B.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: With regard to the first item in schedule B, " wheat in grain," can the minister now give me definite information as to what the British government's attitude will be towards wheat going through American ports?

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I do not think it is possible to add to the clarity of language set forth in article 12 of the regulations made by the British committee, under the Import Duties Act. It was read to the house the other day and I can look it up and read it again if the hon. gentleman so desires. It must be borne in mind by the committee that this is a question which, naturally, is controlled iby the British government, by the regulations passed by that government, which regulations are very clear and well understood. I do not know that it would be profitable to enter into a long discussion of the matter, but I am willing to read the regulation again.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I do not wish to impose upon the minister, but I wish he would read the regulation.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
On a
point of order, Mr. Chairman, I submit that article 4 should be read before schedule B is discussed, inasmuch as one is a qualification of the other.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Article 4 reads:
It is agreed that the duty on either wheat in grain, copper, zinc or lead as provided in this agreement may be removed if at any time empire producers of wheat in grain, copper, zinc and lead respectively are unable or unwilling to offer these commodities on first sale in the United Kingdom at prices not exceeding the world prices and in quantities sufficient to supply the requirements of the United Kingdom consumers.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
May I now reply to my hon. friend from Weyburn by reading article 12 of the regulations under the Import Duties Act:
12. Where empire goods consigned to Great Britain or Northern Ireland have been transshipped en route, or have been shipped from a foreign port after overland transit from the
empire country of origin, the importer at the

Questions
time of making entry will be required to produce the through bill of lading or railway consignment note from the country of production to Great Britain or Northern Ireland in support of the certificate of origin. Where a through bill of lading or consignment note is not available, the invoice, local bill of lading or consignment note from the original point of origin, and a certificate of arrival or landing at, and exportation from, the port of transshipment will be required. Such certificates are to be signed by the proper colonial or foreign customs officer at the port of transshipment, and in the case of the latter the signature must be visaed by the British consular authority. It is essential to prove that the goods were consigned from a part of the empire to Great Britain or Northern Ireland, and not to a foreign country from which they were subsequently reconsigned to Great Britain or Northern Ireland.
Progress reported.
